Bermuda’s New Import Tariff Hits Electrical Equipment Industry

HAMILTON – Bermuda’s Electrical Equipment industry is grappling with the immediate effects of a new import tariff introduced last week by the Ministry of Finance. The measure, which imposes a 20% tariff on imported electrical components and finished products, is designed to bolster local manufacturing but has drawn concern from industry leaders and workers alike.

Firms such as Hamilton Electrics Ltd. and Island Circuitry Inc. have reported disruptions to their production lines, with several key components now subject to higher import costs. “Our inventory costs have risen sharply overnight,” said Marcus Talbot, operations manager at Hamilton Electrics Ltd., whose facility on the outskirts of Hamilton employs 42 people. “We’re reviewing our supply chain and considering adjustments to our product range if the tariff remains in place.”

Employees at the company’s assembly site described an atmosphere of uncertainty. “We’re worried about possible shift reductions,” said one technician, who asked not to be named. “If parts get too expensive to bring in, we might not have enough work.”

The Bermuda Electrical Manufacturers Association estimates that the tariff could increase average unit costs for locally assembled switchgear, circuit breakers, and wiring systems by up to 15%. “With Bermuda’s limited domestic production of core components, our members rely heavily on imports,” said Association president Cheryl DeSilva. “The new tariff places immediate pressure on margins, and some companies may need to scale back operations or delay planned expansions.”

Government officials argue the tariff aims to encourage investment in domestic manufacturing capacity over the long term. “We want to stimulate local production and innovation,” said a spokesperson for the Ministry of Finance, while acknowledging transitional challenges.

Industry analysts caution that the full impact may not be visible for several months. “We are already seeing early signs of production slowdowns and cost-cutting measures,” said trade consultant Julian Masters. “If the increased costs cannot be passed on, there could be further implications for jobs and investment.”

As the new tariff remains in force, Bermuda’s Electrical Equipment firms are closely monitoring developments and assessing their next steps.
